author: Travis
title: KBS Drops a Low-Launch Tour 90, and the Steel Iron Shaft War Gets Another Front
body:
The premium steel iron shaft market has been a two-horse race between KBS and True Temper's Dynamic Gold line for the better part of a decade. KBS just opened a new front in that race.

KBS Golf Shafts announced the Tour 90 on Tuesday, a low-launch, low-spin steel iron shaft positioned as a higher-control alternative to the existing Tour 80. It comes in 90, 95, and 100-gram weights, Stiff and X-Stiff flex, and retails at $34.95. Availability begins April 15 through certified KBS fitters and premium independent retailers.

The technical pitch is a new low-bend point combined with the step-less design KBS has used since the original Tour shaft launched in 2008. Lower bend point at this weight class is a specific design choice. It's a shaft built for the player who's already generating clubhead speed and doesn't need help getting the ball in the air, which puts it in direct conversation with Dynamic Gold Tour Issue X100 and Project X 6.5, not with True Temper's mid-launch offerings. KBS is not trying to broaden its audience here. It's trying to take share inside an already narrow segment.

The historical parallel worth noting: when KBS introduced the C-Taper in 2012, it was a similar play. Lower launch, lower spin, aimed squarely at the tour-level player who had defaulted to X100 for fifteen years. The C-Taper went from zero tour usage to being one of the three most-played steel iron shafts on the PGA Tour within four seasons. That wasn't an accident of marketing. It was a real engineering claim that survived independent fitting data. The Tour 90 is operating from the same playbook, with the caveat that the C-Taper had a wider performance gap to exploit. The space between Tour 80 and a hypothetical Tour 90 is narrower than the space between X100 and what KBS offered in 2012.

The tour count KBS cites, 14 winners and shafts in play across all four majors, is the table stakes for credibility in this category. More telling is the price point. $34.95 keeps the Tour 90 below the $40-plus tier that Project X HZRDUS and some Nippon Modus offerings now occupy, which is consistent with KBS's positioning since founding in 2004. Kim Braly has never tried to win the premium-price game. He's tried to win the played-on-tour game and let retail follow. That strategy has worked. KBS's month-over-month visibility is up 18% heading into a launch window that typically rewards brands with new SKUs in the fitting bay.

The question for KBS isn't whether the Tour 90 will find tour staff users. It will. The question is whether the retail customer who already owns Tour 80 sees enough trajectory difference to justify a reshaft. That's a fitting-bay conversation, not a marketing one, which is exactly where KBS has historically won. Watch the April fitting data, not the launch press. The Tour 90 will be judged by whether it shows up in WITB photos by August, and by whether the C-Taper Lite crowd starts migrating. KBS has earned the benefit of the doubt on shaft launches. The Tour 90 will either reinforce that or expose its limits.

author: Travis
title: KBS Tour 90 Targets the One Gap in Its Own Steel Shaft Lineup
body:
Steel shaft fitting has a weight problem, and KBS just addressed the version of it that lives in the 90-gram range. The Tour 90 is a new low-bend-point iron shaft built for faster swing speeds, added to the KBS Tour family to sit above the existing Tour 80 in weight and below the penetrating-flight options that previously required moving outside the Tour line entirely.

The Tour 90 comes in three weight profiles, 90, 95, and 100 grams, with Stiff and X-Stiff flex options at $34.95 per shaft. That pricing holds the line KBS has kept on the Tour series, which is a deliberate move in a steel market where Dynamic Gold still anchors price expectations and anything meaningfully above that number requires a compelling explanation. KBS doesn't charge a premium here, which tells you something about where the brand wants to compete: volume, tour validation, fitting room default.

The technical case for the Tour 90 is straightforward. Lower bend point shifts the loading zone closer to the tip, which produces a lower launch angle and less spin at the same swing speed. For a player already getting low flight out of the Tour 80 at 80-plus grams, the Tour 90 offers an incremental step toward trajectory control without requiring a move to a heavier shaft like the Tour 105 or a different profile altogether. KBS is filling a gap in its own catalog, which is either responsive product development or a signal that the Tour 80 had a ceiling the fitting data eventually exposed. Probably both.

KBS's tour presence is real. The KBS Tour is one of the most-played steel iron shafts globally, which gives this launch a credibility floor that a smaller shaft brand couldn't claim. When Kim Braly says tour staff asked for this, that feedback loop is legitimate, not theoretical. The KBS fitting network and its presence across all four major tours means the Tour 90 will get evaluated by professionals quickly. Whether it earns bag spots is a different question, but the distribution pipeline to find out is already in place. The brand's DORMIED Index momentum, up 18 percent month-over-month in April, reflects what a tour-validated product story does for brand attention when it's paired with consistent distribution.

The broader steel shaft market is quietly competitive right now. True Temper still owns the volume conversation with Dynamic Gold. Project X has built a strong fitting-room narrative. Nippon has made inroads at the premium end of the steel market in a way that would have seemed unlikely a decade ago. KBS's response to all of that has been to keep the Tour family coherent, to protect its fitting-room relationships, and to release products that answer specific player complaints rather than chase category-level positioning. The Tour 90 is consistent with that approach. It is not a statement product. It is a catalog product, which is exactly what a shaft brand with serious tour penetration should be building in April 2026.

author: Adam
title: Malbon x New Balance: The 997 Becomes a Golf Shoe, and the Sneaker War Officially Hits the Tee Box
body:
Dad-shoe culture and golf were going to collide eventually. Malbon and New Balance just picked the date.

The two brands launch the Bogey Club pack on April 22, a three-colorway run of the 997 silhouette retrofitted with a replaceable cleat system and a waterproof leather upper. Each colorway is capped at 500 pairs globally at $195, with a matching polo and bucket hat available only through malbon.com. The 997 stays mostly intact visually, which is the entire point.

This is Malbon's first footwear-led collab with a performance athletic brand, and the choice of partner says more than the press release does. New Balance spent the last four years becoming the most credible sneaker brand in men's lifestyle, riding Aimé Leon Dore, Joe Freshgoods, and Teddy Santis into a cultural position that Nike used to own by default. Bringing that equity onto a golf course is not a small move. It's New Balance signaling that golf is now a category worth showing up for, the same way Adidas decided basketball was worth taking seriously again.

The 997 was always the right silhouette for this. It's the New Balance shoe that reads as heritage without reading as orthopedic, and the proportions translate to a golf shoe in a way the 990 or 2002R never would. The replaceable cleat system is the part worth watching. Most lifestyle-to-golf footwear conversions stop at adding nubs to a rubber outsole and calling it spikeless. A proper replaceable cleat setup means Malbon and New Balance actually engineered this for play, not just for the parking lot photo.

The $195 price is aggressive but not absurd. FootJoy Premiere leather shoes sit higher. G/Fore retail starts above this. The scarcity play, 500 pairs per colorway, 1,500 total, is where the real margin lives. This will resell. Within a week the StockX listings will look like a Yeezy drop, and Malbon knows it. The brand has been running the streetwear-collab playbook for three years now, with Titleist, FootJoy, and Polo Ralph Lauren already on the resume. None of those moved the needle the way a New Balance collab will, because none of those carry sneaker cultural weight outside golf.

What this actually tells you about Malbon: the brand is no longer pretending to be a golf apparel company that does collabs. It's a collab-engine lifestyle brand that happens to sell golf clothes, and the +31% month-over-month move in the DORMIED Index reflects exactly that velocity. The flagship in LA, the Bogey Club concept, the Hypebeast-friendly drops, all of it is pointed at a customer who shops at Dover Street Market and plays golf on the side, not the other way around.

The risk is the same risk every brand in this lane carries. Lifestyle-first golf brands tend to burn hot for three to five years before the next one shows up with a slightly fresher angle. Eastside Golf is already there. Metalwood is circling. Malbon's answer has been to keep stacking collabs with brands one tier larger than itself, and a New Balance partnership is the biggest one yet. The next logical step is a Nike conversation, and after that there isn't a bigger one. Whether Malbon can keep climbing the collab ladder, or whether it starts building the products that justify being talked about without a partner logo attached, is the question that decides what this brand looks like in 2028.

author: Adam
title: Malbon and New Balance Just Made the Golf Shoe That Doesn't Look Like a Golf Shoe
body:
Three colorways, 500 pairs each, $195 a pop, and a silhouette that was never designed for a fairway. Malbon Golf and New Balance are dropping the Bogey Club pack on April 22: a golf-adapted version of the 997 with a replaceable cleat system and waterproof leather upper, sold simultaneously through select New Balance retail and malbon.com.

The 997 is a deliberate choice, and not an obvious one. New Balance has a deeper performance golf catalog to pull from, and Malbon could have pushed for something newer. Instead they went heritage, which is consistent with what the brand has always been selling: the idea that golf is something you do, not something you dress for separately from the rest of your life. The waterproof leather upper retains enough of the original silhouette that someone who doesn't golf could wear these and nobody would know. That's the point. The replaceable cleat system is the only concession to function, and it's a quiet one.

This is Malbon's first footwear-primary collab with a performance athletic brand, which matters more than the shoe itself. Previous collabs with Titleist and FootJoy kept Malbon in the soft-goods lane. Polo Ralph Lauren kept them in the lifestyle lane. New Balance puts them in a different conversation entirely, one where Nike, adidas, and the broader sneaker market are the reference points. A 997 collab reads on Hypebeast as easily as it reads on a golf forum, and Malbon knows that. The Bogey Club pack is not a golf product with a press release. It's a sneaker drop that happens to be spikeable.

At $195 with 1,500 pairs globally across three colorways, this sells out. That's not a prediction, it's arithmetic. The matching polo and bucket hat, malbon.com exclusive, are the margin play: the people who miss the shoe lottery still have a way to participate in the moment. It's a structure borrowed straight from streetwear drop culture, and Malbon has been running that playbook since they opened the LA flagship. The Bogey Club membership concept exists for the same reason, community as distribution strategy. The brand's DORMIED Index score sits at 15.3 with a 31% month-over-month jump, which suggests this drop is already generating the kind of search and attention that tends to arrive before the product ships, not after.

What this collaboration signals is that Malbon is no longer waiting to be taken seriously as a footwear brand. Two years ago, a Malbon shoe collab meant a FootJoy capsule with a skull logo. A New Balance 997 with a heritage silhouette and a simultaneous sneaker-retail launch is a different ambition entirely. The question going forward is whether the brand can sustain this tier of partnership or whether this reads, a few years from now, like the high-water mark of a cultural moment. Right now, the 997 fits. The harder fit is everything that comes after it.

author: Travis
title: Callaway Just Bought The Data Layer: Arccos Lands $30M and the Fitting Network That Comes With It
body:
Callaway leading a $30 million Series C in Arccos is not a venture investment. It is an acquisition of the data layer that will sit underneath every fitting Callaway runs from now until the partnership ends.

The deal makes Arccos the statistical engine behind Callaway's AI fitting recommendations across 500-plus fitting centers. In exchange, Arccos gets $30 million, doubling its total funding to $60 million, plus what is functionally a distribution moat against every competing shot-tracking platform. Shot Scope, Garmin, and the various app-only entries are now competing for the consumer market while Callaway's retail-and-fitting funnel is locked.

The industry has been here before, and the precedent is instructive. TaylorMade's MyFly app integration with various tracking platforms in the mid-2010s never produced the conversion the brand wanted because the data lived in too many places. Trackman built its fitting empire by owning the launch monitor data end-to-end. What Callaway is doing with Arccos is closer to the Trackman model: control the data, control the recommendation, control the sale. The difference is that Arccos's 12 billion tracked shots come from real rounds, not range sessions, which is a category of data Trackman has never had at scale.

Whether 12 billion shots is the right number to power a fitting recommendation engine is a more interesting question than the press release acknowledges. Most Arccos users are mid-to-high handicaps. The data set skews toward the player who buys fitted clubs, which is convenient for Callaway, but it also means the algorithm is being trained on swings that often have mechanical issues a different shaft will not fix. Equipment optimization based on a flawed swing pattern is a known limitation in fitting, and no amount of Strokes Gained math solves it. The honest version of this technology tells some users their problem is not the 7-iron.

For Arccos, the international expansion language matters more than the funding amount. The UK, Japan, and Australia are three markets where shot-tracking adoption lags the US by roughly four to five years, and where Callaway already has distribution infrastructure Arccos would have spent years building alone. The 22% month-over-month move in the platform's visibility ranking this April suggests the announcement is already doing work, though an 11.2 score on a 100-point scale puts Arccos in the same brand-awareness tier as several DTC putter startups. Capital fixes that faster than product does.

The question Arccos has not answered is what happens to the consumer subscription business when the brand becomes synonymous with Callaway fittings. Independent fitters using Mizuno Shaft Optimizer or Ping nFlight now have a reason to view Arccos as a competitor's tool rather than a neutral data layer. That is the cost of picking a side, and Arccos picked. The next 18 months will show whether the Callaway funnel delivers more users than the independent channel loses, and whether Sal Syed's team can ship product fast enough to justify a valuation that just got considerably more interesting.

Equipment optimization based on a flawed swing pattern is a known limitation in fitting, and no amount of Strokes Gained math solves it. The honest version of this technology tells some users their problem is not the 7-iron.

For Arccos, the international expansion language matters more than the funding amount. The UK, Japan, and Australia are three markets where shot-tracking adoption lags the US by roughly four to five years, and where Callaway already has distribution infrastructure Arccos would have spent years building alone. The 22% month-over-month move in the platform's visibility ranking this April suggests the announcement is already doing work, though an 11.2 score on a 100-point scale puts Arccos in the same brand-awareness tier as several DTC putter startups. Capital fixes that faster than product does.

The question Arccos has not answered is what happens to the consumer subscription business when the brand becomes synonymous with Callaway fittings. Independent fitters using Mizuno Shaft Optimizer or Ping nFlight now have a reason to view Arccos as a competitor's tool rather than a neutral data layer. That is the cost of picking a side, and Arccos picked. The next 18 months will show whether the Callaway funnel delivers more users than the independent channel loses, and whether Sal Syed's team can ship product fast enough to justify a valuation that just got considerably more interesting.",

author: Travis
title: Arccos Just Became the Data Engine Inside Callaway's Fitting Network. That Changes Everything About How the Brand Gets Sold.
body:
Thirty million dollars and a seat inside Callaway's fitting infrastructure is not the same thing as thirty million dollars and a press release. Arccos Golf closed a Series C led by Callaway this week, and the more consequential detail is buried in the second paragraph: Arccos's 12 billion tracked shots will now power the statistical foundation of Callaway's AI fitting recommendation engine across 500-plus fitting center locations.

That is a structural shift, not a product update. Arccos has spent a decade building a shot-tracking platform that most golfers know exists and relatively few actually use consistently. The active user count, 250,000, is real but modest against the scale of the addressable market. The Callaway integration doesn't solve the consumer adoption problem directly. What it does is embed Arccos's data layer into a commercial process that happens whether or not a golfer has ever heard of Arccos. Every Callaway fitting that runs through that recommendation engine is now, functionally, an Arccos data event. That is a distribution solution dressed as a partnership announcement.

The timing has logic behind it. Club Champion built the fitting category into a standalone retail concept over the last decade, and Callaway watched a meaningful share of premium purchase decisions migrate to a fitting environment it didn't control. The Arccos integration is one part of a longer answer to that problem. If Callaway can credibly claim its fitting network produces better recommendations than independent alternatives because it runs on a larger proprietary dataset, that's a differentiation argument grounded in something real. Twelve billion shots is not a marketing number. It's an actual moat, if the recommendation engine is built well enough to use it.

For Arccos, the $30 million brings total funding to $60 million and funds international expansion into the UK, Japan, and Australia. Those markets matter. Japan in particular has a high-engagement recreational golf culture and a current tracking infrastructure that remains underdeveloped relative to the US. Whether Arccos can localize effectively, accounting for swing tendencies, course formats, and app behavior patterns that differ meaningfully by market, is the real execution question. Capital solves the market entry cost. It doesn't solve product-market fit in markets where golf culture runs differently than it does in Seattle.

The DORMIED Index has Arccos at 88th globally with a 22 percent month-over-month momentum gain, which suggests the announcement is generating the kind of attention the brand hasn't consistently commanded. That's notable for a company at this stage. The harder question is whether the Callaway integration converts passive awareness into active users at scale, or whether Arccos remains a platform that industry insiders respect and casual golfers never quite commit to. The fitting integration is the best commercial bet the company has made to answer that question without waiting for organic adoption to do the work. What Callaway does with the recommendation engine output, and whether fitters actually trust it or work around it, is what determines whether this deal matters in five years or just looks good in the announcement.
